newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FEATURE - Chechen war legacy makes polygamy too expensive.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Chechen war legacy makes polygamy too expensive.

text.p: Sharip Batayev's two wives, Valya and Zulpa, labour from dusk till dawn preparing their spartan farmhouse for winter. If the husband they share has his way, however, the backbreaking workload may lighten.
Batayev, showing no signs of fading virility at 59, is one of many Chechen men in the market for third or fourth brides.

While traditional Moslem practices like polygamy have gained in popularity since Chechnya unilaterally declared independence in 1991, the destructive 21-month war with Russia that has now ended has left most people in desperate economic straits.
And although Islamic laws permit men to take up to four wives, the Koran says the husband must be able to provide for them and their children.

"I'd like a nice little girl about 20, preferably with blond hair," laughed Batayev, showing a mouth full of silver teeth and sporting a shiny green Islamic cap with gold embroidery. "Next time can you bring me one from the West?" he joked.
"Who needs you, you old man," shouted Valya playfully from the kitchen in the tiny house.
"I'd take 10 wives if I could take care of them all," Batayev said. "But since the war started we've gone from living well to just getting by."
WIVES DON'T MIND HIM TAKING A THIRD
Batayev's herd of cattle has fallen to two from 10 since 1994 when Russia sent troops to try to crush the tiny republic's independence bid. Most Chechens have no jobs and little money.
Neither Zulpa, 54, nor Valya, 48, would mind sharing their husband with an additional woman.
"Let him have a third wife, or as many as he wants. The more the better. There are the fields to tend in the summer and we could use another pair of hands," says Valya.

Harvesting the family crop of cucumbers, tomatoes and melons became a dangerous business during the past two summers, with Russian warplanes zipping through the sky dropping bombs on nearby rebel targets. Some landed within spitting distance of the modest plot, a few hundred metres (yards) from the house.
COMMUNIST REGIME FROWNED ON POLYGAMY
Polygamy was banned in Soviet times. Batayev and some other Chechen men who practised it risked prison terms for their lifestyles.

"Yeah, people talked. The bureaucrats from the local Communist Party committee asked around town about us. So what? I've always lived by Chechen laws, not by Russian laws. I don't give a damn about what other people think," said Batayev, his face growing stern.
"I only take what has been bestowed upon me by Allah."
Batayev took Zulpa, an ethnic Chechen, as his first wife in 1959 and the couple had two children.
As he was working as a labourer in Sibera in 1971 he met Valya, a midwife in the city of Novosibirsk. He brought her home to Chechnya and had eight more children by her.
Valya, who has mastered the staccato Chechen tongue, and her remaining offspring live on one side of the simple dwelling and Zulpa lives in the other.

"We live as one family. As in any family there are disagreements but there is no jealousy between Zulpa and myself. After all, who could be jealous over such an old man," laughed Valya, dressed in a flowered headscarf.
Some of Batayev's 10 children and eight grandchildren scamper about the house's muddy courtyard in this tiny farming village of a few thousand people 30 km (18 miles) south of the capital Grozny.
ECONOMIC WOES DISCOURAGE TRADITION
When late Chechen leader Dzhokhar Dudayev came to power in 1991 he openly encouraged polygamy.
"Dudayev said take as many wives as you want, and that's what I want to do," said Batayev. But economic circumstances in the wake of the war have put something of a damper on that.

"The Koran says that a man may take up to four wives, but it also requires that he must be able to provide for their material well-being. Today, after the Russians have ravaged our republic with their cannons and bombers, not many of our men can afford such a luxury," said Chechen Mufti Akhmed Khazhe.
Chechen women usually stick to traditional family roles. They are expected to rise slightly or stand up when any man enters a room, be it once or ten times in an hour.
Divorced women are often thought of a second-class citizens and are known by the slightly derogatory term of "zhiru".

Many men consider wedding a zhiru a disgrace, although some Chechen women see divorce as something of a liberation which permits them to shun Chechnya's conservative sexual mores and freely date men without being stigmatised.
YOUNGER WOMEN SEE POLYGAMY AS OUTDATED
But some younger Chechen women, especially in the relatively liberal capital, look down on polygamy as a thing of the past.
"I would never even think of playing second fiddle to some man's first wife. It's horrible," said 24-year old Amiat, serving customers in a small grocery kiosk in Grozny.
But marrying one of the thousands of widows in Chechnya who has lost her husband to the war is considered honourable for a man as long as she does not have young children.
Some religious officials say this could lead to a boom in the practice if the republic can overcome its wartime woes and the economy improves.
"Right now most men have enough problems feeding one wife, let alone two or three," said Khamid Yekhyayaev, an 84-year-old mullah in the small town of Gekhi.
"But if there is work and enough money, I think we'll see quite an increase in polygamy," he said, adding that he had no plans of his own.
